As someone who works on diesel engines and has drove vehicles like this in the military, this game is awesome. The attention to detail is incredible. your tire tracks are permanent even if you made them 5 days ago in some remote part of the map. If you drive in the same ruts over and over it just gets muddier and tougher to get through. I think they actually made the leaf springs bend and flex. Even running over trees is realistic. It truly simulates driving in muddy off-road enviroments. I love how you really have to think about your actions as if you screw up, your only real options are to salvage your vehicl or abandon it (and your hard earned truck-full of lumber).

They did an incredible job on this game.

My son said he's got a game he thinks I'd be interested in so I watched him play Mudrunner. He has the ability to make hard things look easier than they are and he made Mudrunner look, not easy but at least do-able, and I thought it looks like fun and a challenge so ok I'm in.
At first I found it hard, frustrating, too much for me and almost gave up, but when I got over this and discovered other trucks to use, better ways to do things and I began to understand the maps, I felt a lot more comfortable and confident. And so, unknown to me at the time, my addiction began.
I became competent then more experienced and now I have a truck, the Oshkosh M977, that will take me anywhere I want to go with a trailer and combined value of 8 points per load, so there's just one load to each mill. I fell in love with the brutality of the wilderness and became obsessed with the isolation from humanity, and wanted so much to actually be there, and this is my fantasy;

I live here and this is my job. Whichever map I go to my garage has all the mod cons of home; a fully equipped kitchen and bathroom with electricity, running water, plenty of toilet paper (wouldn't want to run out of that out here) and a big bedroom for my comfortable queen-size bed. I get food and all my supplies dropped in once a week by chopper and I'm here all by myself, all alone, no people, and loving it! I'm totally in awe of my new existence and can't get enough, even when I'm going to sleep at the wheel and running of the road I'll wake up and keep going, even start a new map, because I just don't wanna leave.

Oh, and of course, I also have the best gaming computer and in my spare time when I'm not fighting with the environment and delivering logs, I can play Mudrunner.

The advertising for this game does not represent the basic gist.  MudRunner is a logging simulator. You retrieve logs using trucks and various logging cranes in Russian wilderness in the 1960s.  The natural landscape is unknown to you and the usable vehicles are hidden.  You go through a process of adventure-and-discovery to find the vehicles and deploy them. 

Nothing in this game is scripted  as it is a simulator.  Crazy, unexpected events take place merely due to the laws of physics.   The decisions you make have consequences and there is no [i]Game Over[/i] here to save you. Any mistakes require recovery with ingenuity.  When trucks turn over they are stalled in distant forest. You must bring in larger trucks to perform  "heavy rescue"  with wenches.

[b][i]Spintires: MudRunner[/i] is an odd duck, I tell you.[/b] This is a slow burner if I've ever seen one. I've never played a driving-based game where you move sooooo slowly before. But it works. Before I booted it up, I envisioned romping around in the mud and wilderness with trucks with big tires. Nope. You *crawl* at a snails pace around the world in vehicles few will recognize.

[i]Essentially, you are in a remote wilderness sandbox and you perform fetch quests.[/i] The 'game' aspect is not getting stuck. It's not easy, I assure you. The maps are not infinite, but are very beautiful. It's a fairly lonely experience (I've only played single player). There isn't a story or any of that. It's weird. I also don't recognize any of the vehicles, and I suspect that's the same for nearly anyone outside this niche line of work. Controller works really well with this. 

This is an oddly zen experience, but you have to choke down an hour or so of [i]'what the heck is this'[/i] kind of feeling. 

[b]Pros:[/b]
+Oddly zen experience
+Nothing else quite like this game out there
+Controller support is great
+The graphics are amazing and the download is less than a gig? Fantastic
+Steam Workshop support is nice here

[b]Cons:[/b]
-This is not for everybody; you are given a sandbox to play around in so keep this in mind - you get out what you put in
-The 'hook' is not something I immediately felt; I needed to play a good bit

[b]Really interesting title that is welcome in my library.[/b] Full price is a bit steep, but hey, you could get alot out of this one.

Update, February 20th 2026: One must imagine sisyphus trucking

MudRunner is a game where you take a 1980s Soviet truck and drive it directly into the Earth’s crust while trying to deliver logs. Not gold, not medicine—logs. Trees you chopped down, and now must lovingly return to the forest. It’s eco-ironic.

You start the game with a truck that handles like a sleepy walrus in rollerblades. You think, “This won’t be so bad.” And then—mud. Not just any mud. The kind of mud that has opinions. The kind of mud that grabs your tires and says, “You live here now.”

Every mission is a slow, squishy battle between you and gravity. You’ll spend 45 minutes hauling three sticks across terrain that looks like it was designed by a sadistic oatmeal monster. You’ll try to cross a river, misjudge the current, and suddenly your truck is doing synchronized swimming.

There’s no music. No flashy HUD. Just engine sounds, occasional bird chirps, and the distant laughter of the developers watching you try to reverse uphill in a hurricane made of dirt. It’s pure vibes, and the vibe is: “You should’ve brought the winch.”

Also, there’s no tutorial. The game throws you in like, “Here’s a truck. Here’s a bog. Figure it out, comrade.” And you do. Eventually. After crying. Twice.

Multiplayer is where friendships go to die beautifully. You’ll all meet up to rescue Dave’s truck from a ravine, only for everyone to also get stuck. Now it’s a convoy of sadness. You form a daisy chain of winches, each vehicle screaming through the mud like a cursed conga line of diesel-powered despair.

Final score: 10 foggy forests and 3 existential breakdowns per log drop-off.
MudRunner is what you play when you want to feel the thrill of achieving absolutely nothing very, very slowly—and somehow love every painful, sludgy second of it.

This is my first experience with the Spintires games; I never played the first one. I'm not a car guy, not into the whole 4x4 thing, the concept of the game didn't even interest me plus the bad press on the first game didn't help the image. Never gave the game much thought after that untill I saw a review of Mudrunners yesterday. The guy playing was just having a blast, and I like the European/American Truck Simulator games so I thought "why not?".

Went through the tutorial (which needs a little more meat on it) and jumped into the campaign. My first delivery attempt ended with my truck lying on its side in a river. The second attempt ended with the same truck on its side in a creek. Ok, this isn't working. Grabbed one of the other trucks that I had found just sitting in the woods and tried again. My third delivery attempt made it through. WOOOOOO! 

Mission complete but the other half of the map was still black. Now how do I open that up? And that's where the game got me. All the "how" I was doing. "How do I get there?" "How did I get stuck and now what the hell do I do about it?" "Do I run with bigger loads that are more difficult to get through or save myself some headache with smaller loads and just make more trips?" "Found a new garage, but how do I open that up?" It was only my first few hours into the game and I had already got my $30 worth out of it; I was having a blast!

Yeah I struggled with the camera at first like most people probably do but I quickly adapted to it. It doesn't bother me that it's difficult to position the camera at an angle high above and behind the vehicle because I rarely care what's far ahead of me. What I need to know is what's underneath me and immediately in front of me and what are my tires doing. The camera works very well for that. My tires tell me everything I need to know and the camera gives me that information just fine.

Most of the graphics are nice and I really enjoy the details I've noticed. The mud building up on the tires and then washing off after going through water. The mud and water splash on the sides of the vehicle, or the way the water flies off rapidly spinning tires. The barely visible heat haze from the engine and the way the exhaust changes depending on engine damage. The way the tires deform from the terrain and running over rocks/trees. There's just some nice touches here.

My first 10 hours have all been spent on the first map and I'm not done yet. I got smart and used my Jeep to open the rest of the map up. I discovered more logging camps and another garage. I discovered how to open that garage and while trying to take a shortcut to the mill, I discovered disaster. I got stuck. The S T U C K type of stuck. The tree ahead of me was just out of range of my winch and those on either side just kept trying to tip my load over. I was so mired in the mud that I couldn't move an inch either forward or back. Felt like a dinosaur in a tar pit. 

That's when I discovered how to change vehicles and how to pull another vehicle free, but not without tipping the whole thing over and losing the load. All that time trying to make it back was wasted, but I was still happy. Why? Because I finally discovered what that "Diff Lock" button does.

1. Bring logs through swamp
2. Get stuck
3. Bring another truck
4. Get stuck again

10/10 would bring another truck again

P.S. Recommended for people who likes vehicles especially heavy machinery and tired of competitive games.

After the debacle of OOvee it is great to see this game get a decent publisher. It could have easily faded away which would have been a shame. I do not and probably never will know the actual facts of what happened between Oovee and the developer, and I honestly don't care. I am just glad that Spintires has finally got the release it deserves and will (hopefully) continue to recieve updates. I have to commend Focus on stepping in and allowing this to happen.

While some owners of the original may be peeved at having to repurchase what is essentialy the same game, I do not have a problem with it. Focus having taken on the publishing of the game deserve some recompense and the discounted price they offer to owners of the original is more than fair as far as I am concerned.

The improvements in the game are subtle but veteran drivers will notice them. The physics are improved and the new water effects are great. The sounds of the trucks and the environment have also had an overhaul. The interface has had some minor improvements and the introduction of a tutorial will be welcomed by newcomers.

An in-cab view has been added, but unfortunately in its current form it looks like a tacked on afterthought and is rubbish. It looks like something out of an early 90's game and the mirrors do not work. Hopefully this will be rectified in a future update. This view is something I was looking forward to, but at the moment I just cant bring myself to use it without shaking my head and thinking how sad it is.

The camera in the original was something that a lot of players did not like. I personally never had a problem with it, but still used Spintires+ to improve the control of it. The same camera mode has been retained in this version, but seems more restricted than the original, it can be a bit difficult to get it into the perfect position without it flicking off to another angle. This is something that will most likely annoy many people but is hopefully another thing that gets improved with an update. A 'free' camera mode would also be a welcome addition.

The addition of 'challenges' is most welcome and is hopefully something that gets expanded on, and hopefully we get new 'official' maps and challenges with updates. Workshop support is available from release with a few vehicles already present. It would be nice to be able to install user created maps and challenges through the workshop and I hope this is something that the developer implements.

Overall I thoroughly recommend Mudrunner. If you do own the original but did not enjoy it or play it much then you will not find anything here to improve that situation. If however you own the original and enjoyed it then I believe that it would be worthwhile purchasing this, it is the game that the original should have become. If you didn't own the original and the idea of driving Russo truck through wild muddy terrian sounds interesting then you will definately enjoy this.

+ Game looks nicer and has new graphical features (mud sticks to your tires now, water looks much more realistic, large trailers have hookups to the cab, to name a few), and sounds just as good. The new music is kinda meh, first thing I did was disable it honestly.
+ The game runs a lot smoother, haven't had any framerate hickups at all on a GeForce 750 ti.
+ New developers = More money for Pavel (who deserves it) = More updates
+ 6 [strike]all new[/strike] maps, and a few more trucks and attachments.
+ UI improvements look great
+ I feel like the camera is a bit better now, and less likely to have you suddenly staring at the sky or be really zoomed in. I could be wrong though and I'm just a bit better at it than before. It still operates in the same way, if you were wondering.
- Still not perfect though, could definitely benefit from more camera angles/styles, like a classic chase camera for easy driving along a road when you can go faster.
- Interior view now exists, but... needs some work and is kind of ugly... Apply more polish here and it'll be great.
- [strike]Kinda wished we could still play the old maps, but oh well. I'm sure they'll be added as a mod[/strike]. EDIT: Some of the original maps remain, but under different names.
+ Oh yeah, they're most likely going to add maps to the Steam Workshop soon, so yay for that!

Overall, if you were a fan of the original, you will undoubtedly be a fan of this and should definitely support it. If you are angry about it being the exact same game, educate yourself on the games history, and support the one guy who made the game rather than the dkheads who took his money and ran.

I thought this game was hard, and then I played Snowrunner. The two games are arguably quite similar with Snowrunner being much more user-friendly w/much more surface level features and Mudrunner being the more difficult, more simulator-driven game. But the reality is that the maps in Mudrunner are only a fraction of the size of the maps in Snowrunner with the only tasks in Mudrunner being delivering logs, whereas Snowrunner has a massive collection of things that get delivered. For the time that it was released, Mudrunner was an awesome title that built upon the success of the original Spintires game. The reality is that now in 2022, Snowrunner has completely superseded Mudrunner and this game is much less of a good buy. If you can catch it on sale, by all means it is a solid game with decent driving mechanics, bland but passable graphics, and unmemorable sound design. There is plenty of mud to get stuck in and birds to scare away with your horn. If you have the money though, just pick up Snowrunner.

I desperately want to give this a positive review. But I can't. Not compared to the original, anyway. I'll just list some pros, cons, and personal disappointments for now I guess.

Pros:
-It looks considerably prettier
-The physics are much more impressive
-The interior camera is excellent
-All of the cameras seem a bit better
-There are new engine sounds, with better variety
-More default trucks, and better ones
-The UI is much nicer
-Little things like visual indication of diff locker and engine starting is nice (though an option to shut them off would also be nice)
-The game, of course, is a ton of fun
-Gamepad controls are vastly better (though I don't use one, it's nice)
-There are a few nice features added, like the border checkpoints and a better winching system
-The game is much, much better optimized, and runs wonderfully (with one caveat, as explained next)

Cons:
-On my machine at least, the game is EXTREMELY unstable. I have a gaming laptop with an i7 and an 800 series Nvidia GPU, I'm well above the system requirements, and I've verified the cache and redownloaded the game several times. The game just isn't stable for me, mods or not.
-It does look prettier, but not THAT much prettier. The vehicles are better and of more consistent quality, and lighting effects are dramatically better, but ultimately terrain looks about the same
-Wheel/tire customization has been removed
-Many, many vehicle attachments and customizations have been removed
-Multiplayer is disabled when using non-vanilla maps
-Both single and multiplayer maps are locked behind completion of objectives, with no apparent way to unlock them without doing so (old one had all open, and frankly I don't enjoy actually logging)

Disappointments:
-Manual transmission mode is still almost entirely worthless. I was really hoping they'd implement something like ETS2/ATS or BeamNG, where you can use buttons to shift up and down, but they retained the same system from before, which is sad.
-Rocks are still bizarrely slippery, rock crawling still looks doable but pretty much isn't.
-I'll reiterate again how much it bugs me that wheel and tire changes have been removed. Maybe if I complain enough they'll add it back.
-The game in general appears to want to make you play it as a logging simulator. I enjoy it simply as an offroad simulator. For me, this is a limitation of the way I used to enjoy to play the game, and definitely a disappointment.



In general, I just don't feel like I *got* anything for my money honestly. I loved the original, and I want to love this, but between the crashing, the removed features, and the general lack of any compelling reason to play this over the original, I'm just left feeling almost like I've gotten scammed. It's the same game, with some features removed. Given that the original looks almost as good, is more stable, and has more options, I really have to recommend anyone looking at this game to go buy the original instead. At least at this point, the original has far more mods available as well (though I'm sure that will change over time). So that's my verdict. Maybe, just maybe, this time Pavel will stay with a publisher, and updates will be released making the game more stable and more fun, and some of my complaints will be addressed. It has been stated that wheel and tire customization may be brought back if there's demand for it, so hey, who knows. But right now, as of November of 2017, given Pavel's (and Focus's) prior history, I do not have high hopes for future updates, and in its current state the game is ultimately a disappointment.

MudRunner Review

Games are great because they let you do anything or be anyone. You can be Aloy, an adventurous warrior adept at killing robotic animals in a far-flung future. You can explore entire planets and travel through a vast galaxy in No Man’s Sky. In Everything, you can be, well, anything. In Spintires: Mudrunner, your goal is to move logs around a particularly muddy patch of land.

That’s perhaps a little unfair of us, though. This is an impressive off-road simulation title that, while on the surface may appear dull as dishwater, is surprisingly compelling. As we said, the basic objective in the main game is to traverse treacherous terrain in heavy duty vehicles, delivering timber from A to B. It sounds like a simple enough task, but there are a number of factors working against you.

One of them is the brilliant physics simulation at the heart of Mudrunner. The trucks are slow, heavy things with a convincing weight and realistic suspension that reacts as you’d expect to the conditions at hand. Equally, the mud and water react dynamically to your vehicle as you drive. Deep tracks are carved in the muck as you push through, your tires clogging with earth and slipping in the increasingly poor conditions. Water displaces realistically and washes the mud from your wheels. Rivers have currents that can force you off course or tip you over if you’re not careful.

Expect the modding community to explode more than the original now that the developer is back in full control.

Let me start by simply saying I've never in my life driven a large truck in the wildernesses of Russia and points abroad. 
But let me also say that if I ever had to, Mudrunner has given me an excellent sense of preparedness. 

This game lets you play in the mud with vehicles most of us have probably never heard of. There's a joy and a beauty in that I've yet to find from another game. But don't let the looks fool you. This is almost purely a game of logistics. You need to scout watchpoints to open up the maps, usually a smaller vehicle is suited for that. Find fuel. Carry some with you or have some nearby. I like to have a capable medium-sized truck around with a cistern or a fuel trailer so I can use it as a checkpoint when using my heavies to haul large loads of logs across the map. 

Every bog is a puzzle. You have to be constantly scanning the area for a saving tree to make sure you can get out if you're mired. Worse case scenario, you can always bring a bigger truck or tractor to drag your stuck butt out. There are times you have to fight for every meter you drive. But the reward, the achievement of pulling tons of logs across a rushing river, your heart in your throat as the current threatens to topple your trailer and make your last hour of work all but naught is as exhilarating a feeling I've ever had playing a video game. Once you set up a system of repair trucks and fuel and logging operations, you feel a sense of accomplishment. You've tamed the great wilderness, it bends to your will. 

The looks in the game are spectacular. Mud sticks to tires and flings off at speed, it squishes and splotches and acts lifelike. Exhaust billows out in greys and whites, sometimes sparks if you're a poor driver or you find one heavily damaged in the wild. Trees bend and sway with the gentle breezes. Almost all of the trucks aren't rigid machines. Torque will make the entire truck flex. Driveshafts spin, leaf springs compress, the poor guy getting tossed around the cab will lean back and fall asleep if you're stopped at night. The vehicles are your weapons, your tools, and they feel very much alive.

The sounds are great, turbos whine, gears click and pop, every truck seems to have its own soundtrack, and if its reused its because it has the same motor. Creeks and rivers babble, mud makes its ghastly noise as 45" tires tear into it with any form of success. Nature is at work. Birds flutter away from bushes when the horn honks, crickets chirp at night, the list goes on. (Though I miss in the free beta the sound of gears grinding and a guy screaming profanities in Russian, hopefully that will make a return someday.)

Multiplayer co-op is fun. I play with a friend of mine and one of us will scout and do search and rescue while the other unlocks garages, or goes logging. Understandably, the engine only renders your vehicles while it will only show the other player's active vehicles, and the rest are "ghosts" with labels. This is one of my only gripes about this game, most modern computers can handle four player's vehicles all active in the map without too much effort. The game engine is very smooth and seems to be pretty well optimized, I don't see why it is that way but oh well. My buddy will just have to believe me when I'm pulling a Ural with long logs through a bog with my recovery-built E-7310. 

In closing, is this game for everyone? No, maybe not. This is a puzzle game uniquely disguised as a driving game. You will work as much as you play sometimes, especially if you get some friends along for the ride. If you like trucks, mud, getting stuck and the thrill of getting un-stuck, I recommend this game wholeheartedly.

Spintires: MudRunner (STMR)….a game where players simulate performing what is surely among the most unpleasant, dangerous, dirty, sweaty, bug-infested and frustrating jobs on Earth; wilderness logging driver. Sound awful? (It is!) Additionally, at least for single-player mode, one can hardly imagine a game less exciting for spectators (at least for the majority of gameplay.) Yet it’s an exceptionally popular indie game, and I can personally confirm there is challenge and excitement to this game that has rarely been experienced in the thirty-some years I’ve been PC gaming.

STMR is basically as described above. Using realistic heavy-duty vehicles, each with specific features, a player (or players) attempts to collect, then deliver, already cut timber to lumbermills. Simple enough, if fuel wasn’t being rapidly consumed, or support vehicles weren’t crucial for a number of reasons, and mud, swiftly running rivers, bad roads (often no roads), darkness of night, mountains and vehicular damage didn’t plague almost every inch of each lengthy endeavor. (Please be aware of two things in this review: 1) It’s written as if STMR had NO predecessor (avoiding all inherent drama), and 2) while one may suspect STMR is even MORE fun (and more reasonable and realistic) in multiplayer mode, this review is written from single-player experience only.)

STMR is a BEAUTIFUL game, very often approaching photo-realistic graphics. STMR physics is phenomenal, though by no means perfect. For example, spinning wheels while stuck in mud tends to “stuck” one worse IRL, but not in STMR. Also, the same deep mud road should be more difficult to pass on subsequent trips, but isn’t, though that seems something that could add substantially to gameplay and strategy. And having limited, specific camera choices may have seemed like a good idea, it doesn’t really work very well. And watching the winch cable pass through any trees not attached to gets old fast. And I REALLY wish my vehicle wasn't repeatedly damaged by diffariential use on the "hard surface" of a sandy beach or a muddy road.

Initially, STMR is a strategy game. Every action is preceded by thoughtful analysis of the task ahead; which vehicle(s) would be most suitable, what areas of the map may yet need to be opened, the choice of which features need to be added to each vehicle to provide fuel, repair and assistance, what size/distribution of load is best (or necessary), how to most safely transport that load over what route, considering accessibility to resources (and dangers. A short route is frequently far the riskier.) Nothing is simple, and by the time that ignition key is turned, a chess match with nature has already been played in each “driver’s” head. (Never fear! It’s actually far more intuitive than it may sound, and the necessarily lengthy and fun tutorial (called “Challenges”), is excellent.)

SO, why is STMR such a rewarding game? Perhaps time has lead this reviewer to an answer. Most games consist of actions that lead players to conflict. STMR spends almost every moment already IN conflict. Every inch of travel is a battle of man and vehicle against multitudinous forces of nature (and physics.) A choice of roadway over finding/forcing one’s way through a thick forest can lead to a choice of conflict, and a choice of solutions. When one finds the mud too great an obstacle, should they; 1) use driving techniques (such as rocking) to get free, 2) downshift for more power 3) engage differential for more traction, 3) engage the winch, front or back, 4) call for the assistance of another vehicle, and perhaps the various “tricks” some can provide, 5) drop a load or trailer to lighter the load, 6) combinations of those options listed, 7 - ?) any number of other creative options. Few games offer so many challenges (or at such an unrelenting pace.) And all that simply to progress another TEN FEET! (At least in this example. While this no doubt sounds excessively frustrating, it’s actually some of the more interesting, challenging and rewarding of all that STMR offers.) While at minimum, completion of each map is all that’s required, there are numerous actions tracked within STMR that can be used by each player to measure performance and additionally compete. STMR is really only over when each player wants it to be over, and replayability is sort of the whole point.

Ultimately, STMR is about POWER! When that vehicle is beyond axle-deep in the mud and the winch is attached to a hundred year old tree, it’s a battle of (metaphorically speaking) “man against the planet Earth”, and Earth quite often wins. But when the power of the truck combined with the power of the winch is engaged by the player’s hand, something inside feels the power inherent within that struggle, and is at one with it. Perhaps it might be most accurate in comparing the player to Iron Man, and his truck is Iron Man’s suit. IN STMR, the driver is very much a superhero!

A review could describe literally hundreds of features, details and aspects of gameplay, but perhaps it’s best to explain, “Why play Spintires: MudRunner?”, and perhaps this review has achieved some degree of success. STMR is numerous games, and each player need find that part of STMR that is most appealing personally. It’s NOT for everyone, and should never be presented, or considered, as such. However, there’s no question that’s it’s “for” this reviewer, and for very many other gamers, and may be for you as well. It’s a game that includes an excellently paced learning curve, and I imagine most players will know how they feel about it within the Steam two-hour limit for refunds. Be aware that a measure of STMR’s realism is that you will very possibly feel exhausted by a long game session, and sleep well that night.

This is a driving / offroad fan's dream game. If you're looking for a quick comparison of old Spintires vs MudRunner, MudRunner is essentially the old game, except the controls (when using a controller) are a lot better. Everything seems fined tuned and a little smoother. However, you are essentially buying the same game with a few tweaks. 

The [b]gameplay[/b] is pretty rocksolid and does provide for some interesting challenges. Although it may seem mundane and boring to drive around in the dirt, make one small mistake and all your progress can go up in smoke. I was really close to delivering logs when I happened to go over a bridge. I cut a corner a little too close and my entire trailer and truck flipped over. Things can change pretty quick, especially when you are not paying attention. Spintires is an offroad open sandbox game complete with 5 maps and about 7-8 different trucks. Now, the idea of it being sandbox may throw some off - but oddly enough there is enough going in this game to keep you busy. The game concept follows around objectives and the process of driving up to garages and trucks to unlock them. Some (or most) objectives require you to transport certain materials such as lumber. Not all trucks can carry lumber and not all trucks have the attachments to. When starting off at your main garage, players can modify their vehicles by adding utility carts, lights or such other accessories. The trucks that are put into this game are pretty cool and quite dynamic. Some are stuck without all wheel drive while some have differential locks as well as all wheel drive. Even though this is the second version of the game, it would have been nice for them to add other objectives besides lugging wood around. 

Trucks can be as small as a jeep, to as big as a heavy crane truck you would see helping unload construction material near a job site. Some trucks even come with cranes to load and unload lumber! There is, however a draw-back to this awesome inclusion. Typically, you load up your lumber automatically and only if you happen to get into an accident or logs fall out, then you can use your crane to load them up. So the crane does have a use, but can also be seen as useless to some. The driving experience itself is addicting. I'm not sure why, and I'm not sure how, but the challenge of ripping through dirt road, water, mud, even rolling over sticks or the occasional rock is amusing. Adding a cart to the back of the truck also makes the challenge that much harder as it's not only the truck you have to get across the river. The driving itself seems quite realistic to me. I have also seen a lot of reviews saying it is ridiculous how some trucks have the hardest time going over rocks or even loose tree branches. 

Although it can be the case, typically the trucks shouldn't have too much of an issue going over the obstacles. Tree branches aren't too bad but the rocks will definitely set you back. I wish there was a bit more freedom within this realm to go over obstacles, but going through trees that haven't matured quite yet is pretty fun (disclaimer : I don't ride my Toyota through any tree, shrub or the sort. I love mother nature).  Sometimes where the is no path, a path can be made with a heavy truck pushing small trees aside. Most collisions feel right except one little thing that bugs me, why can't I drive into an exploding barrel that was put on the map? I know it's kind of silly to have such a thing next to a lumber yard, but why put it there if I can't "use" or hit it? The game has weird moments like this where it chooses to clip instead of let you collide. What I absolutely do love about this game is the winch. When I first started, I was extremely frightened to go at it alone as I would end up on my side or get stuck. I started learning how to use the winch efficiently and my experience with the game got a lot better. I'm glad I chose to play multiplayer first in lieu of single player. The community was a worldly and friendly one. Multiplayer WILL NOT save your  progress but single player WILL. 

[b]Graphics[/b] are quite nominal especially when it comes to the mud and water. Trees are there but I think could have been done a bit better. Back drops are nice, would have been nicer with some mountains or something else to fill some gaps. The game also features a night and day scheme. Compared to the original Spintires, the visuals are a little better all around (trucks to environment). The [b]sounds[/b] are actually on point, and when your vehicle is physically damaged, damaged sounds also follow. 

I like this game, it could have been better with a bit more variation and a few more construction touches (crane's and the like... maybe even dirt diggers), none the less, pretty good game to some, decent for others. I would love to see more map additions and truck additions and a little variations on objectives.

I have tried a few mods and they work quite well with the game. I would suggest keeping an eye out for which ones you use as some of the achievements in game may get disabled. 

I got this game for ~$15 and would say it's worth it. $30 may be slightly over stretching it for a few.

This game is very good and extremely unique.  But it's different than what the trailers show.

The trailers paint a very loud, intense picture, but that's not what's going on during gameplay.  This game is mostly quiet, peaceful, and very methodical.  There are moments of intensity, like an unplanned tumble down a hill, or rescuing your friend with an urgent and clenching winch pull.  But those moments are the exception, not the norm.

Instead, after planning a strategy to get the right trucks and resources in the right places, you spend most of your time carefully and quietly navigating beautiful and immersive environments in fascinating vehicles.  Mudrunner is as much an atmospheric puzzle game as it is a driving simulation game.  Off-road adventure driving just happens to be the puzzle medium, which is why this game is so unique.  To be successful in the higher difficulty levels, you need to be careful figuring out how to navigate the next section of terrain, and reading the landscape to figure out where the conditions might be favorable for the particular truck and load you're driving. "How deep is the soft mud over there before it gets to the hard stuff?  How should I angle my trailer in this river so that I don't get flipped over where the current is strong?  How hard can I stay on the throttle here without sliding sideways into that low spot?"  Anyone who's driven heavy equipment in remote areas will feel right at home in this game, and anyone who hasn't will learn a lot.

Most off-road games are a fast-paced smash through the woods, and some off-road sports are actually like that.  But this game captures the isolating unknowns of being truly off the beaten path, with vehicles only just capable of moving through the diverse terrain.  In those situations, even slow and careful is an exciting challenge.

----
As an aside, at least 10% of my brain is dedicated to being continuously blown away at the simulation realism of the trucks and terrain whenever I play this game.

There is no story, and you don't hold progression between maps other than your ability to play new maps and different trucks.

Multiplayer is vastly improved over the first game, but it's still missing some features like shared trailers and shared headlights so you can see eachother's winched pull and their headlights in the woods.  There's a few other minor nitpicks too, but for gameplay it's massively improved.  No more heavy desync, much better multiplayer winching, and collision between players (with their currently active vehicle, anyhow.)

Challenge modes are fun and offer a few hours of enjoyment by the looks of it.  I've sank about 30 minutes into two of them, with 9(?) total.  Challenges in the challenge modes get pretty zany and seem like it's going to be a blast.

Camera controls are mildly improved, and I mean mildly.  It's mostly the same.  If you hated it, you hate this one still.  They added a cab view, and it works nice.  Has a custom UI for each truck too.

Custom map support is supposed to finally be coming to the workshop, so we should see easier application of maps in the future.  Currently not a plus or minus, just a personal note.

Overall it feels worth my money thus far as a veteran of the series.  I've gotten about 100 hours out of the original as a casual singleplayer, I'll probably do about the same with MudRunner, but this time enjoying some solid multiplayer since it works better.  Here's to hoping I'm not wrong, or I'll feel bad for having mislead you guys.  :(

Definitely the best off-road driving game of all time! Has the most realistic off-road mechanics out there, especially how the mud works as well as the "spintires" effect. I especially like the setting in the wilderness of Siberia using old Russian trucks. 

Bear in mind that this game is a simulator. You will be spending hours just driving slowly through the most inhospitable and difficult terrain imaginable. A part of the challange is managing gas consumption and the roles of different vehicles (e.g. you will combine the uses of a scout jeep, lumber truck, crane truck, fuel truck, recovery vehicle etc.) but the real adventures happen when you get into some trouble, like getting stuck in deep mud or flipping your vehicle and needing to fix the situation (e.g. by using a recovery vehicle to tow the damaged truck back to the garage). 

One of my most memorable moments was getting stuck deep in the middle of a huge river crossing. Damn, it took a lot of effort and many damaged vehicles to recover the lumber truck from the river. These kinds of realistic situations and problems are very satisfying and challenging, something you don't get often from video games or simulators in general. I myself have been on many off-road jeep tours in real-life (in Iceland) and gotten into these kinds of situations (getting stuck high up on a mountain or in a glacial river etc.) and these moments from the game impressively reminded me of those real-life situations.

So if you are like me, and this is what you're into, then go for Spintires: Mudrunner.
Keep in mind that you should get this game and not the previous version (this one is supported by the developer while the older one is not).

Owners of this game and Spintires are like the kids in a divorce, and we just found out the reason we haven't heard from Mom over at the original is because dad's been hiding all her messages. Me, I'm just psyched we get double presents at xmas
